## Scope

This review surveys the published literature on adsorbents used for the drying of gases, taking in 147 papers that have appeared over the last 9 years. The field it covers is the removal of water vapour from gas streams by passing the gas over a solid material that takes up the water preferentially, holding it on and within the solid until the material is regenerated and the water is driven off again. The gases concerned are those of ordinary industrial practice, including air supplied to instruments and processes, natural gas being prepared for transport and sale, and a variety of process gases whose moisture content must be brought down to a low level in order to protect downstream equipment, to prevent the formation of solids within pipelines, or to meet a specification attached to the gas as sold. The adsorbents within the scope of the review are the families of materials that are used for this purpose in practice and studied for it in the literature: silica gel, activated alumina, and the zeolite molecular sieves, together with newer materials that individual papers propose as candidates for the same duty. The review is concerned with performance in service as much as with capacity in the laboratory, and it therefore includes papers on regeneration, on the ageing of beds in cyclic operation, and on the behaviour of adsorbents in the presence of the contaminants that real gas streams carry, alongside the much larger number of papers that report uptake measurements on fresh material under controlled conditions. Papers concerned solely with the synthesis of new materials, without any measurement of water uptake, fall outside the scope, as do papers dealing with the drying of liquids or of solids, and papers in which adsorption is used to remove some component other than water.

## Established results

Across so large a body of work, a number of findings recur so consistently that they may fairly be regarded as established. It is established, in the first place, that the quantity of water an adsorbent takes up at equilibrium rises steeply as the partial pressure of water vapour in the gas increases from low values, and that the shape of this rise differs characteristically between the material families: the zeolite molecular sieves take up a large share of their capacity at very low partial pressures, which is what fits them for drying a gas to very low moisture contents, whereas silica gel takes up relatively little at low partial pressures and reaches its capacity only as the gas approaches saturation, which fits it instead for removing the bulk of the water from a wet gas. It is established, secondly, that capacity falls as temperature rises, so that a bed dries best when it is kept cool, and that regeneration is correspondingly carried out by heating the bed, by reducing the pressure over it, or by sweeping it with a dry purge gas, the water being expelled as the conditions that favoured uptake are reversed. It is established, thirdly, that the rate at which water is taken up is governed not by the equilibrium capacity but by transport: by the movement of vapour through the gas film around each particle, and by diffusion within the particle toward the surfaces on which uptake occurs, so that particle size and gas velocity influence the length of bed that a given duty requires even where they do not influence the amount the material can ultimately hold. It is established, finally, that contaminants in the gas stream degrade performance: heavy hydrocarbons, oils and other strongly held species occupy capacity and foul surfaces, and beds in real service lose working capacity over their lives even where the fresh material, as characterised in the laboratory, appears entirely satisfactory. These findings are supported by the great majority of the 147 papers taken together, and no serious body of work within the review contradicts any of them.

## Disagreements

The literature is considerably less harmonious when it turns to the quantitative comparison of the material families, and the quantity on which reports principally conflict is the equilibrium water uptake of the zeolite molecular sieves at low partial pressures of water vapour, the very region of operation on which their reputation rests. Some groups report capacities in this region that are markedly higher than those reported by other groups for materials that are nominally of the same type, and the discrepancy between the highest and lowest reported values is large enough to reverse the ranking of materials that a designer would draw from the literature taken at face value. The disagreement does not appear to be a simple matter of error on one side or the other. The conflicting reports differ systematically in the conditions under which the measurements were made: in the pretreatment and activation of the samples before measurement, in the temperature at which uptake was recorded, in the manner in which the partial pressure was established and held, and in whether the uptake was measured by following the weight of the sample or by following the moisture content of the gas passing over it. Each of these choices is defensible in itself, and some of them are known to shift the measured uptake, but because the choices vary from group to group in combination rather than one at a time, the literature does not at present allow the discrepancy to be assigned to any single cause. There is a secondary disagreement, less sharply drawn, concerning the working capacity that should be expected of silica gel in bulk drying service, where reports differ over how much of the equilibrium capacity remains available once the dynamics of a real bed, with its incomplete regeneration and its ageing, are taken into account. Until the measurement conventions in this field converge, or until a round of measurements is made on shared samples under shared conditions, quantitative rankings drawn from different groups' reports will continue to carry an uncertainty that the individual papers, each internally consistent, do not disclose.

## Gaps

The most striking gap in the literature is a measurement that, on the evidence of the 147 papers surveyed, nobody reports: the water uptake that an adsorbent retains after extended regeneration cycling under a realistic humid feed. Papers report the capacity of fresh material in abundance, and a smaller number report capacity after some ageing or after exposure to a named contaminant, but a systematic record of how the drying capacity of a bed declines, cycle by cycle, over the long sequence of adsorption and regeneration steps that constitutes its working life, is essentially absent. The omission matters because the economics of gas drying turn on precisely that decline: the interval at which a bed must be changed, the energy consumed in regenerating it throughout its life, and the moisture excursions experienced by the downstream plant as the bed ages are all governed by the cycling behaviour that the literature does not measure. A second gap lies in the reporting of the conditions under which uptake was measured: pretreatment of the sample, in particular, is described loosely or not at all in a substantial minority of papers, which renders the disagreements described in the preceding section needlessly difficult to resolve after the fact. A third gap concerns mixtures: almost all measurements are made with water vapour in a clean carrier gas, whereas the industrial duty involves water in the presence of hydrocarbons and other adsorbable species whose competitive uptake shapes the performance of the bed, and measurements under such mixed conditions, over cycling, on the materials in ordinary use, would do more to advance the practical design of gas drying than further refinements of single-component capacity on fresh samples.

## Scope

This review covers adsorbents for gas drying in 147 papers from the last 9 years. Gas drying is the removal of water vapour from a gas stream by a solid that takes up the water and holds it until regeneration drives it off. The gases in scope are those of ordinary practice: air for instruments and processes, natural gas prepared for transport and sale, and process gases whose moisture must be brought low to protect downstream equipment, to prevent solids forming in pipelines, or to meet a sale specification. The adsorbents in scope are the families used and studied for the duty: silica gel, activated alumina and the zeolite molecular sieves, with newer materials that papers propose as candidates for the same duty. Performance in service is in scope alongside capacity in the laboratory, so papers on regeneration, on bed ageing in cyclic operation and on behaviour in the presence of carried contaminants stand beside the larger number that report uptake on fresh material under controlled conditions. Papers on synthesis without a water-uptake measurement are outside the scope, as are papers on drying liquids or solids and papers on removing a component other than water. The review treats the established families as the centre of the field and the candidate materials as its margin, because service experience, supply and regeneration practice attach to the established families, and a candidate is of interest chiefly as a possible replacement for one of them on a named duty. Duties are compared on the moisture content to be reached and on the continuity of the service, since a bed that dries deeply but regenerates slowly answers a different need from a bed that dries moderately in a rapid cycle.

## Established results

Four findings recur across the literature and stand as established. Equilibrium water uptake rises steeply with the partial pressure of water vapour, and the shape of the rise differs by family: zeolite molecular sieves take up a large share of their capacity at very low partial pressures, which fits them for drying to very low moisture contents, while silica gel takes up little at low partial pressures and reaches capacity only as the gas approaches saturation, which fits it for bulk water removal. Capacity falls as temperature rises, so a bed dries best cool, and regeneration is carried out by heating the bed, by lowering the pressure over it, or by sweeping it with dry purge gas, reversing the conditions that favoured uptake. Uptake rate is governed by transport, not by equilibrium capacity: by vapour movement through the gas film around each particle and by diffusion within the particle, so particle size and gas velocity set the bed length a duty requires without changing what the material can ultimately hold. Contaminants degrade performance: heavy hydrocarbons, oils and other strongly held species occupy capacity and foul surfaces, and beds in real service lose working capacity over their lives even where fresh material characterises well in the laboratory. The great majority of the 147 papers support these findings, and no serious body of work in the review contradicts them. The established findings also fix the vocabulary of the field. Capacity without a stated partial pressure and temperature is not a comparable quantity, and working capacity, the share of equilibrium capacity a real cycle can use between regenerations, is the figure by which beds are actually sized. Reports that keep the two apart can be set side by side; reports that merge them cannot, and much of the apparent scatter in the literature is a scatter of definitions before it is a scatter of materials.

## Disagreements

Reports conflict on one named quantity: the equilibrium water uptake of zeolite molecular sieves at low partial pressures of water vapour, the region on which their reputation rests. Some groups report uptakes in this region markedly higher than other groups report for materials nominally of the same type, and the spread between the highest and lowest values is large enough to reverse the ranking of materials a designer would draw from the literature at face value. The disagreement is not simple error on one side. The conflicting reports differ systematically in measurement conditions: in sample pretreatment and activation before measurement, in the temperature of the measurement, in the way the partial pressure was established and held, and in whether uptake was followed by sample weight or by the moisture content of the gas passing over the sample. Each choice is defensible, and some are known to shift the measured uptake, but the choices vary between groups in combination rather than one at a time, so the literature does not allow the discrepancy to be assigned to a single cause. A secondary disagreement concerns the working capacity of silica gel in bulk drying: reports differ on how much of the equilibrium capacity survives the dynamics of a real bed, with its incomplete regeneration and ageing. Until measurement conventions converge, or shared samples are measured under shared conditions, rankings drawn across groups carry an uncertainty that the individual papers, each internally consistent, do not disclose. The disagreement also has a geography of method: groups that measure gravimetrically tend to report the higher uptakes, and groups that measure by the gas phase tend to report the lower, which suggests that part of the gap is carried by the measurement chain rather than by the samples. Neither chain is self-evidently the truer one, since each converts its raw observation into an uptake through its own assumptions about dead volume, buoyancy and the dryness of the reference state.

## Gaps

On the evidence of the 147 papers surveyed, the measurement nobody reports is the water uptake an adsorbent retains after extended regeneration cycling under a realistic humid feed. Fresh-material capacity is reported in abundance, and capacity after some ageing or after exposure to a named contaminant appears in a smaller number of papers, but a systematic record of drying capacity declining cycle by cycle over a bed's working life is essentially absent. The omission matters because the economics of gas drying turn on that decline: the bed change interval, the energy spent regenerating the bed over its life, and the moisture excursions passed downstream as the bed ages are all governed by cycling behaviour the literature does not measure. A second gap is the reporting of measurement conditions: sample pretreatment is described loosely or not at all in a substantial minority of papers, which leaves the disagreements above needlessly hard to resolve after the fact. A third gap concerns mixtures: nearly all measurements use water vapour in a clean carrier gas, while the industrial duty is water alongside hydrocarbons and other adsorbable species whose competitive uptake shapes bed performance. Mixed-feed measurements, over cycling, on the materials in ordinary use would advance practical design further than further refinement of single-component capacity on fresh samples. The gaps are connected. Cycling measurements on mixed feeds, reported with pretreatment stated in full, would at one stroke supply the ageing record the economics require, test the established findings under service conditions, and give the disagreement over low-pressure uptake a set of shared samples on which methods could be compared directly. The literature has the instruments for such work; what it has not yet produced is the work itself, and the absence is the more notable because every party to the disagreement would benefit from its removal.
